t.1.2.1: Having heard those words of Nārada, the great sage, righteous of soul and skilled in speech, together with his disciple, paid him honor.
t.1.2.2: Then the divine sage Nārada, duly honored by him, took his leave and, being permitted to depart, went away into the sky.
t.1.2.3: A moment after he had gone to the world of the gods, the sage then went to the bank of the Tamasā, not far from the Jāhnavī.
t.1.2.5: O Bharadvāja, behold this bathing place free of mud, lovely, its waters clear like the mind of a good man.
t.1.2.4: Having reached the bank of the Tamasā, the great sage, seeing a bathing place free of mud, spoke to the disciple standing at his side.
t.1.2.7: Thus addressed by the great-souled Vālmīki, the disciplined Bharadvāja handed the bark garment to that sage, his teacher.
t.1.2.8: Taking the bark garment from his disciple's hand, he, with his senses restrained, wandered about, gazing on every side at that vast forest.
t.1.2.6: Let the water-pot be set down, dear son, and let my bark garment be given to me. I shall bathe right here in this most excellent ford of the Tamasā.
t.1.2.9: There, near that spot, the blessed one saw a pair of krauñca birds, inseparable, wandering about and uttering sweet cries.
t.1.2.10: But from that pair, a Niṣāda, bent on evil and a dwelling-place of enmity, struck down the male one while he looked on.
t.1.2.11: But his mate, seeing him struck down, his body drenched in blood, writhing upon the ground, cried out in a piteous voice.
t.1.2.12: Seeing that bird thus struck down by the Niṣāda, compassion arose in that righteous-souled sage.
t.1.2.13: Then, out of his compassionate nature, the brahmin, thinking "This is unrighteous," and seeing the female krauñca bird weeping, spoke these words.
t.1.2.14: O Niṣāda, may you never attain a firm place for endless years, since you slew one of this pair of krauñca birds while it was lost in love.
t.1.2.16: Reflecting, that greatly wise and thoughtful one formed a resolve in his mind; and that bull among sages spoke these words to his disciple.
t.1.2.15: As he spoke thus and looked on, a thought arose in his heart: "Stricken with grief for this bird, what is this that I have uttered?"
t.1.2.17: Bound in metrical feet, even in its syllables, and fit to be sung to the rhythm of the stringed lute, this utterance that came forth from me as I was stricken with grief shall be called śloka and nothing else.
t.1.2.18: But the disciple, delighted, received the excellent words of that sage as he spoke them, and his teacher was pleased with him.
t.1.2.19: Then, having performed his ritual bath at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rule, the sage turned back, pondering that very matter.
t.1.2.20: Then Bharadvāja, the humble and learned disciple, took up a full water-pot and followed behind his guru.
t.1.2.22: Then Brahmā came, the self-existent lord and maker of the worlds, the four-faced one of great splendour, to see that bull among sages.
t.1.2.21: Having entered the hermitage grounds together with his disciple, the knower of dharma sat down, and though he held other conversations, he remained absorbed in contemplation.
t.1.2.23: Then Vālmīki, seeing him, rose up at once, restraining his speech; with joined palms and composed in spirit, he stood there, utterly astonished.
t.1.2.25: Then the blessed lord, having seated himself upon a most highly honoured seat, thereupon directed the great sage Vālmīki to take a seat.
t.1.2.24: Bowing duly to him and asking the imperishable one whether he was free from ailment, he worshipped that god with water for the feet, the guest-offering, a seat, and words of praise.
t.1.2.27: A grievous wrong has been done by this wicked-souled one whose mind is set on enmity, who would kill, without any cause, such a sweet-voiced krauñca bird.
t.1.2.28: Grieving again and again for the female krauñca bird, he, having become inwardly absorbed and wholly given over to sorrow, sang this verse once more.
t.1.2.26: Then, when the Grandfather of the worlds himself had taken his seat, Vālmīki, his mind still dwelling on that very event, sank into meditation.
t.1.2.29: Then Brahmā, smiling, said to that bull among sages: "It is indeed a śloka that you have composed; there need be no deliberation about this."
t.1.2.30: By my will alone, O brahman, has this speech come forth to you. Compose the entire story of Rāma, O best of sages.
t.1.2.31: Narrate the story of Rāma, the righteous-souled, virtuous, wise and steadfast one in the world, just as you heard it from Nārada.
t.1.2.32: Whatever took place, both in secret and in the open, concerning that wise Rāma together with Saumitri, and concerning the Rākṣasas, in every detail…
t.1.2.33: And whatever befell Vaidehī, whether in the open or in secret, all of that too, though unknown, will become known to you.
t.1.2.34: In this poem of yours, no word of yours shall ever be untrue. Compose the sacred and delightful story of Rāma, bound in ślokas.
t.1.2.35: As long as the mountains and rivers shall stand upon the surface of the earth, so long shall the story of the Rāmāyaṇa be spread throughout the worlds.
t.1.2.36: As long as the story of Rāma composed by you shall be told, so long shall you dwell in my worlds, above and below.
t.1.2.37: Having spoken thus, the blessed Brahmā vanished right there. Then the sage Vālmīki, together with his disciples, was filled with wonder.
t.1.2.38: Then all his disciples sang this śloka again and again, and, delighted and greatly astonished, they spoke out.
t.1.2.39: The grief that the great sage sang forth in four quarters of equal syllables, through its being repeated again and again, attained the state of a śloka.
t.1.2.40: This thought arose in Vālmīki, whose self was cultivated by meditation: "Let me compose the entire Rāmāyaṇa as a poem in verses such as these."
t.1.2.41: Then the renowned sage of noble intellect composed, in hundreds of ślokas with even syllables, delightful and noble in metre, meaning and words, a glory-bestowing poem about this illustrious Rāma.
